title_original: THE SECOND COMING OF A FIRST-RATE FAILURE

blocks.text: The boy who cried woof, the artist who drank the Kool-Aid, and other professional embarrassments.
Adilson De Oliveira

The contemporary artist is a peculiar animal. He spends months begging to be let into a room, then suffers a nervous collapse when somebody finally opens the door. The exhibition goes well, the audience applauds, the institution congratulates itself, and the artist returns home feeling like a dog that has successfully chased a car and discovered he has absolutely no fucking idea what to do with it. The photographs are online. The curator has caught a flight. The artist lies in bed, examining his career as though it were a suspicious growth. He has achieved something. He is miserable. Adilson De Oliveira, The Boy Who Cried Woof. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.caption: Adilson De Oliveira, The Boy Who Cried Woof. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.text: Worse, he is embarrassed about being miserable, which gives him something new to be miserable about. They call it the post-exhibition blues, a diagnosis so offensively mild it sounds like a jazz quartet playing in a shopping centre. The reality is closer to withdrawal. For months the artist has been sustained by urgency, panic, deadlines and the flattering illusion that everything depends upon him. Then the opening happens. The audience leaves. The work continues without its maker, and the maker discovers that he has mistaken being busy for being necessary. The institution has a programme. The artist has a nervous system. Only one of them is expected to function after the exhibition.

I recently exhibited Church of the Holy Prompt at Maputo Fast Forward, a religious farce about Prompt Jones, a failed artist who becomes a preacher because nobody gives a damn about his art. Jones discovers that people will believe almost anything provided the speaker has a microphone, a congregation and sufficient confidence to ignore the evidence. His church promises salvation through artificial intelligence, which seems reasonable in a world increasingly determined to automate the last remaining inconveniences of human judgement. I made the exhibition to ridicule the business of manufactured faith. Unfortunately, I had overlooked my own subscription.

For the first time in my career, somebody gave me actual money to make an exhibition. Funding. A production budget. The sort of thing other artists discuss casually while I try to determine whether an invoice will arrive before the electricity gets disconnected. I was genuinely grateful. Naturally, I responded by behaving like a man who had been entrusted with the nuclear codes. The exhibition involved holograms, projections, equipment and an international border. Every technical inconvenience became a constitutional emergency. I developed a personal grievance against electricity.

Then the fucking thing worked. The film played. People arrived. There were compliments, conversations and the familiar spectacle of cultural revolutionaries drinking somebody else’s alcohol. Somebody may even have watched the entire fourteen-minute-and-forty-three-second video, an act of endurance for which I remain eternally grateful. I was delighted. For approximately fifteen minutes, I was the happiest idiot in Mozambique. Adilson De Oliveira, Empty Talk. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.caption: Adilson De Oliveira, Empty Talk. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.text: Then I got catastrophically drunk. And then drunk again. Cocaine entered the proceedings and began issuing philosophical statements through my mouth. I explained the collapse of civilisation to people who had probably only asked where the bathroom was. By midweek I was drinking to celebrate the exhibition, drinking to recover from celebrating it, and drinking because sobriety threatened to introduce questions I had travelled internationally to avoid. The worst part was that some of it was tremendous fun. Maputo was wonderful. The people were wonderful. I was having the time of my life while conducting an increasingly expensive experiment in personal degradation.

The mornings were less magnificent. My mouth tasted like a municipal accident. Every conversation returned for prosecution. I considered Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous and, during a particularly violent episode of professional despair, alternative employment. AA. NA. A job. Three possible futures, each more terrifying than the last. I briefly imagined becoming an accountant, until I remembered that accountants have to understand money. I had spent months making something worth remembering and was now doing everything possible to forget the week in which it had succeeded.

And all the while, I kept drinking the Kool-Aid. Which is especially irritating because Jim Jones didn’t even use fucking Kool-Aid. At Jonestown in 1978, the poisoned drink was prepared with Flavor Aid; many of the victims were coerced, and hundreds were children. Yet popular culture turned the atrocity into a cheerful expression for blind obedience. Even the metaphor is fraudulent. I know this, and I keep drinking the fucking stuff. I drink it when a curator tells me exposure is valuable. I drink it when an institution explains that the opportunity is its own reward. I drink it when somebody suggests the next exhibition will change my life. The flavour is irrelevant. The obedience is the product.

I recognise this arrangement because I have been a drug addict. There is a peculiar intimacy between an addict and his dealer. The dealer understands your landlord, your rental agreement, your financial difficulties and why your wife is leaving you. He listens to your grievances, remembers your name and agrees that everybody has treated you terribly. You begin to believe the bastard loves you. Perhaps he does, in some limited commercial sense. But every conversation ends with you handing over money and promising to return. The art world has perfected a remarkably similar relationship. The institution understands your struggle, sympathises with your sacrifices and assures you that your practice is important. Then the exhibition ends, the budget closes, and you are left with the same financial problems and a powerful desire to see your dealer again.

This is the unpleasant machinery behind the post-exhibition blues. Artists invest months of labour, anxiety and personal significance in events that last a few hours before becoming somebody else’s administrative responsibility. During production, every decision matters. The artist is indispensable. Then the opening happens, the curator moves on, and the person who made the work is suddenly redundant. The body finally registers the exhaustion. The mind interprets it as failure. The artist starts looking for another exhibition to cure the effects of the previous one. We have built a profession in which the treatment for withdrawal is another dose. Adilson De Oliveira, Barking Up The Wrong Tree. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.caption: Adilson De Oliveira, Barking Up The Wrong Tree. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.text: Philip Guston understood something about the violence of artistic judgement. In 1970, he exhibited his new figurative paintings at Marlborough Gallery in New York, abandoning the language that had established his reputation as an Abstract Expressionist. Critics attacked him. Hilton Kramer was particularly savage. His friendship with Morton Feldman fractured. Guston subsequently travelled to Italy, where he continued working through the consequences of having made a serious artistic decision in public. I admire Guston to the point of illness. I want to be Guston. Violently. I want his conviction, his courage and his ability to sit in a studio making paintings that might offend everybody he knows. Unfortunately, I possess neither the environment nor, if I am being sufficiently unpleasant with myself, the commitment required to paint with that degree of sustained seriousness. Guston returned to painting. I returned from Maputo and considered accountancy.

The distinction is considerable. Guston made paintings that changed the course of his work. I made a fraudulent preacher, got drunk in Mozambique and wrote an essay about feeling sorry for myself. Art history will survive the omission. Still, his experience exposes an uncomfortable truth: even an established artist can be wounded by the public response to his work. Recognition offers no permanent protection against doubt. James Ensor had his own bruising encounters with criticism in the 1880s; Edvard Munch’s Berlin exhibition was closed amid scandal in 1892. These histories are far more complicated than an opening-night hangover, and I have no intention of inviting myself into their company. I merely admire the furniture.

The art world, meanwhile, is burning with remarkable elegance. Institutions organise conferences on precarity while artists struggle to pay rent. Curators discuss care, sustainability and resistance over excellent wine. Everybody is interrogating something. The biennale has become an international gathering of people committed to dismantling systems of power while observing the seating arrangements at dinner. Artists complain about exploitation, then accept another invitation. We denounce institutional vanity, then check whether our names appear in the press release. We know exposure does not pay the electricity bill. Then somebody offers us an exhibition and we behave like starving dogs hearing a tin opener.

I have become the boy who cried woof. The boy who cried wolf warned the village of a danger that eventually arrived. The boy who cried woof is considerably less useful. He is the dog himself, barking at every institution, critic, collector and curator, announcing the imminent collapse of contemporary art while quietly hoping somebody will invite him inside. He bites the hand that feeds him, apologises for the inconvenience and asks whether there might be another canapé. He has spent years warning everybody that the art world is a fraud while trying desperately to become one of its beneficiaries. The village has stopped listening. The dog has started writing criticism. Adilson De Oliveira, Hitting the Gate, Not the Gatekeeper. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.caption: Adilson De Oliveira, Hitting the Gate, Not the Gatekeeper. © Adilson De Oliveira.

blocks.text: And here I am, preparing the refreshments. The art world is burning, the guests are discussing institutional responsibility, and I am in the kitchen carving imaginary strips from my own love handles, frying them in the fat of professional resentment and arranging them on a silver tray. A little self-loathing, some financial insecurity, a garnish of critical theory. Would madam care for a canapé? Locally sourced. Artist-produced. Entirely sustainable. I have spent years turning my own humiliation into material, then complaining that nobody wants to consume it. I am the chef, the livestock and the starving customer. Somewhere a curator is preparing a statement about the radical potential of self-sufficiency.

The trouble is that artists genuinely love what they do. They work themselves into the ground making things that may never receive recognition, and when something finally succeeds, they discover that public approval cannot settle a private argument. The exhibition was good. The people were generous. The opportunity mattered. None of that prevented me from feeling like shit. My exhaustion was real, my chemical behaviour was stupid, and the professional insecurity waiting beneath it was older than the exhibition. The institution did not create every problem in my life. It simply provided a temporary structure in which I could avoid looking at them.

Prompt Jones understood the arrangement perfectly. He became a preacher because nobody cared about his art. He offered salvation to people who wanted somebody else to tell them they mattered. I constructed him as a warning and then spent an entire week behaving like a member of his congregation. I wanted the exhibition to prove that the years of work, financial sacrifices and professional uncertainty had been worth it. More embarrassingly, I wanted it to prove that I was worth something. No exhibition can survive that expectation. No curator should be expected to provide that service. Even the most sympathetic dealer eventually wants to close shop.

And there is one final humiliation. Nobody agreed to review the fucking show. I constructed an entire religion, transported its prophet across an international border, staged the apocalypse in Maputo and failed to persuade a single critic that the occasion warranted three hundred words.

Andy Warhol supposedly advised that one should weigh reviews rather than read them. What the fuck does that even mean? Weigh them? By the kilogram? Am I supposed to arrive at the gallery with a kitchen scale and determine my historical importance according to the combined mass of printed criticism? Is a savage three-page review worth more than a complimentary paragraph? Does Artforum paper stock carry greater intellectual authority than a provincial newspaper? If Robert Hughes calls you a cunt in six hundred words, does that constitute a greater artistic achievement than being praised by somebody nobody has heard of?

I would be delighted to conduct the experiment. Unfortunately, nobody reviewed the fucking exhibition. I have nothing to weigh. Warhol could afford to disregard the contents of his reviews because there were enough of them to constitute a measurable physical substance. Guston could retreat to Italy knowing his paintings had provoked an actual critical argument. I would have welcomed a bad review. Call the exhibition derivative. Call the film indulgent. Call the artist a technologically assisted fraud with an inflated sense of his own importance. I would have read every word, complained about the critic’s incompetence and quoted the review in my next funding application.

And so the circle closes. I have spent this entire essay attacking the machinery of artistic validation while quietly hoping somebody might consider the attack worth publishing. I have denounced the artist’s appetite for recognition while arranging that desperation into paragraphs. I have exposed Prompt Jones as a fraud, only to discover that his creator has developed an almost identical business model. The boy who cried woof has finally stopped barking long enough to eat himself. Prompt Jones became a preacher because nobody cared about his art. I became an essayist because nobody reviewed mine. Warhol weighed his reviews. Guston survived his. I have had to write my own.
Five stars. A devastating examination of contemporary narcissism. The artist should be institutionalised. Preferably by a major museum.

Adilson De Oliviera joins the ART AFRICA team as a guest writer while taking up a long-term fellowship with the ART AFRICA Foundation. Working closely with Suzette and Brendon Bell-Roberts, he focuses on developing new outlets for critical art writing and helping to develop young voices within ART AFRICA ’s Programme.

Adilson De Oliveira is a Johannesburg-born multidisciplinary artist, animator, and cultural practitioner whose work explores history, memory, and Luso-African identity through satire, technology, and decolonial critique. A Fine Arts graduate from the University of the Witwatersrand, he began as a printmaker before shifting toward a practice that treats machines as creative collaborators. Since co-founding The Magolide Collective in 2019, De Oliveira has used media such as drawing, video, XR, and AI to challenge the Western art canon and blur the boundaries between truth and fiction. His work serves as both a resistance and an archive, capturing the complex realities of postcolonial South Africa.
